title: Brahma metu mām: the first trisuparṇa
theme: The first of three passages called trisuparṇa: a prayer that brahman, the sweet, come to the speaker; an offering of the breaths to Soma; and a brāhmaṇa passage on giving and reciting it.

words.gram: n. nom. sg. as printed (Vedic form for brahma)
words.context: Sāyaṇa: «ब्रह्मं परब्रह्मतत्त्वं मामेतु प्राप्नोतु» — may the supreme brahman come to me

words.gram: n. nom. sg. as printed (Vedic form for madhu)
words.context: Sāyaṇa: «मधुं परमानन्दलक्षणमाधुर्योपेतं वस्तु» — the thing whose sweetness is the highest bliss
The anonymous commentator: «मधुरं ब्रह्मैव मामेतु, न त्वन्यत्क्षुद्रदैवतादिकमिति भावः» — brahman alone, not some lesser deity
The anonymous commentator: «हे सोमोमा ब्रह्मविद्या तया सह वर्तमान परमात्मन्» — Soma read as sa + Umā: the supreme self with Umā, the knowledge of brahman
The anonymous commentator: «देवमनुष्यादयः» — gods, men and the rest
Sāyaṇa: «वत्सो बाल एतासां त्वदीयप्रजानां मध्ये बालवदहं त्वदीयकरुणायोग्यः» — a child among your creatures, fit for your compassion

words.role: relates the speaker to the creatures
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «ता अभिलक्ष्य» — with regard to them
Sāyaṇa: «स तादृशस्त्वत्सेवकोऽहं» — such a one, your servant
Sāyaṇa: «संसाररूपस्य दुःस्वप्नस्य घातक परमेश्वर» — slayer of the bad dream that is saṃsāra

words.gram: as printed: voc. sg. or imperative (see morphology)
words.context: Sāyaṇa: «दुरुष्षह दुःखमुत्कर्षेणाभिभव। वर्णविकारश्छान्दसः» — overpower sorrow utterly; the change of sound is Vedic

words.gram: pron. m. acc. pl. as printed

words.context: Sāyaṇa: «त्वदीयाः प्राणवृत्तयो याः सन्ति तान्वृत्तिप्राणांस्त्वयि जुहोमि प्रक्षिपामि» — the movements of breath that are yours, I cast into you
Sāyaṇa: «विषयेभ्य इन्द्रियाणि निरुध्य त्वदेकचित्तो भवामीत्यर्थः» — restraining the senses from their objects, I fix my mind on you alone
Sāyaṇa: «शिष्ययाच्ञामन्तरेणैव ब्राह्मणायोपदिशेत्» — teach it to a brāhmaṇa even without the pupil’s asking
Sāyaṇa: «त्रिसुपर्णमन्त्रं सर्वदा जपन्ति» — constantly repeat the mantra
Sāyaṇa: «सोमयागं प्राप्नुवन्ति» — the soma sacrifice; Bhāskara: «सोमं परं देवं सोमयागफलं वा» — the supreme god Soma, or the fruit of the soma sacrifice
Bhāskara: «सहस्त्रपुरुषायां ब्राह्मणपङ्क्तौ श्राद्धादिषु भुञ्जानास्» — eating at a śrāddha in a row of a thousand

sandhi.rule: The m is joined to the following vowel.
n becomes ñ before a palatal (P. 8.4.40 (स्तोः श्चुना श्चुः)).
prāṇān + tān → prāṇāṃs tān (P. 8.3.7 (नश्छव्यप्रशान्)); the Taittirīya recitation writes the nasal as ग् (प्राणाग्स्ताञ्).
vai + ete → vā ete: ai becomes āy and the y is dropped (P. 6.1.78 (एचोऽयवायावः), P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य)).
brāhmaṇāḥ + trisuparṇam → brāhmaṇās trisuparṇam: the visarga becomes s before t (P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः)).
ā and sahasrāt are written as one; final t stays before p.

sandhi_exceptions.note: saḥ · aham: printed so aham, the o and the a kept apart without elision (classical so ’ham). A Vedic hiatus (prakṛtibhāva, P. 6.1.115 (प्रकृत्यान्तःपादमव्यपरे)); every witness prints it so.

morphology.note: brahman is a neuter n-stem whose nominative is brahma; the text has brahmam, and madhum beside madhu. Sāyaṇa glosses the forms as they stand: «ब्रह्मं परब्रह्मतत्त्वं» and «मधुं परमानन्दलक्षणमाधुर्योपेतं». Bhāskara divides differently, brahma metu mām, taking metu from a root mī ‘go’ («मी गतौ»), and rejects the view that the m is an inserted Vedic sound (see ambiguities).

Sāyaṇa takes it as an imperative of √sah with dur- and ut-, ‘overpower utterly’, the sounds changed in the Vedic way; the anonymous commentator as a request to destroy unbearable existence («दुःसहं भवं विनाशयेत्यर्थः»); Bhāskara, with a different reading, as ‘hard to overcome’, said of the speaker who has won knowledge («ज्ञानलाभेन अनभिभवनीयः सम्पन्नोऽस्मि»).
In the second yās te soma line the relative is feminine plural beside the masculine prāṇān tān; the agreement is loose.

translation.literal: May brahman come to me. May sweetness come to me. May brahman itself, the sweet, come to me. Which are your creatures, Soma — towards them I am a calf, that one, I. O slayer of evil dreams, overpower! Which are your breaths, Soma — those I offer. One should give the trisuparṇa unasked to a brāhmaṇa. These truly destroy [the sin of] killing a brāhmaṇa. The brāhmaṇas who recite the trisuparṇa attain soma. They purify the row up to a thousand. Om.
translation.readable: May Brahman come to me; may the sweet come to me; may Brahman itself, the sweet, come to me. Soma, among your creatures I am your child. You who destroy the bad dream, overcome it. Soma, the breaths that are yours I offer back to you. This trisuparṇa should be taught to a brāhmaṇa even unasked. Those who recite it, the text says, destroy even the sin of killing a brāhmaṇa; they attain soma; they purify a row of a thousand at the meal. Om.

anvaya: ब्रह्मम् माम् एतु । मधुम् माम् एतु । ब्रह्मम् एव मधुम् माम् एतु । सोम, याः ते प्रजाः [ताः] अभि सः अहम् वत्सः [अस्मि] । दुष्ष्वप्नहन्, दुरुष्षह । सोम, याः ते प्राणान् तान् जुहोमि । त्रिसुपर्णम् अयाचितम् ब्राह्मणाय दद्यात् । एते वै ब्रह्महत्याम् घ्नन्ति । ये ब्राह्मणाः त्रिसुपर्णम् पठन्ति ते सोमम् प्राप्नुवन्ति । [ते] आ सहस्रात् पङ्क्तिम् पुनन्ति । ओम् ।
syntax: Three short imperative prayers with etu; then an address to Soma with a relative clause (yās te … prajāḥ) and a verbless statement about the speaker (vatsaḥ … so aham); two vocatives; a second relative clause with a first-person verb (juhomi). The brāhmaṇa part that follows uses an optative of instruction (dadyāt) and present statements in the plural, the subject of ghnanti (ete) left general.

ambiguities.note: Sāyaṇa (and the anonymous commentator, who glosses «मामेतु प्राप्नोतु») read brahmam etu mām, ‘may brahman come to me’. Bhāskara divides brahma metu mām, metu from a root mī ‘go’, and rejects the view of ‘some’ that the m is an inserted Vedic sound («छान्दसो मकारोपजन इत्याहुः»). The words of the text are the same either way.

The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa read Soma as sa + Umā, the supreme self with knowledge; Bhāskara gives several derivations, among them the lord of all («ईष्टे सर्वस्येति सोमः») and the one with Umā, the power named by Om.
Sāyaṇa: ‘such a one, I [am a child] towards your creatures’. Bhāskara also considers reading abhisaḥ as one word, ‘the one who presses [soma] all round’.

metre.name: mixed
metre.note: Prose formulas and a brāhmaṇa passage, with an anuṣṭubh in the middle (Bhāskara: «यास्त इत्यनुष्टुप्») that is irregular as printed: yās te soma prajā vatso ’bhi so aham has 12 syllables, duṣṣvapnahan duruṣṣaha 8, yās te soma prāṇāṃs tāñ juhomi 10.

beginner: This is the first of three short passages that share the name trisuparṇa, ‘the three fine-winged ones’. It begins with a simple prayer: may Brahman come to me, may the sweet come to me, may Brahman itself, the sweet, come to me. Then it speaks to Soma, whom the commentators take as the Supreme together with knowledge: among your creatures I am like your child; you destroy the bad dream; the breaths that are yours I give back to you. Sāyaṇa reads this last line as drawing the senses back from their objects. The passage ends with a few prose lines about the text itself: it should be taught even to one who has not asked, and the text promises those who recite it freedom from the gravest sin. The edition reports these claims; it does not make them.
analogy: Like a child who brings a gift back to the parent who gave it, and calls it an offering.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: A threefold prayer that brahman, the sweet, come to the speaker; a statement to Soma that the speaker is a child among his creatures and offers him the breaths; and a brāhmaṇa passage: the trisuparṇa is to be given unasked to a brāhmaṇa, its reciters destroy the sin of killing a brāhmaṇa, attain soma, and purify a row of a thousand.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Bhāskara: three anuvākas to be recited for the destruction of all sin, known and unknown: «अज्ञातप्रज्ञातसमस्तपापक्षयार्थं जप्यास् त्रिसुपर्णाख्यास् त्रयोऽनुवाकाः». He derives the name from suparṇa, the fine-winged bird, and takes the bird as Om itself, the bird on which the self flies up to brahman («प्रणवः शकुन्तः सुपर्णः शोभनपतनः»); that is why each of the three ends in Om («प्रणवप्राधान्यमेषां दर्शयितुं त्रयाणामनुवाकानां प्रणवान्तत्वम्»). The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa introduce them as mantras that remove the sins that obstruct knowledge: «अथ ज्ञानप्रतिबन्धकब्रह्महत्यादिपापनिवृत्तिहेतवस्त्रिसुपर्णनामका मन्त्रा उच्यन्ते».

commentary.q: How is the offering of the breaths read?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa: the movements of breath belong to the Lord, who made them, so the speaker withdraws them into him, holding the senses back from their objects and fixing the mind on him alone: «विषयेभ्य इन्द्रियाणि निरुध्य त्वदेकचित्तो भवामीत्यर्थः». Bhāskara similarly: «आददे प्रत्याहरामि विषयेभ्यः» — I take them back from the objects.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa: other teachings follow the rule that one should not speak unless asked («नापृष्टः कस्यचिद्ब्रूयात्»), and are given when the pupil requests them; this one is to be taught to a brāhmaṇa even without the request: «इमं तु त्रिसुपर्णमन्त्रं शिष्ययाच्ञामन्तरेणैव ब्राह्मणायोपदिशेत्».

commentary.q: What is the Om at the end?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa: it shows that the deity of the trisuparṇa is the supreme self named by Om: «तस्मादों प्रणवप्रतिपाद्यः परमात्मैव त्रिसुपर्णमन्त्रस्य देवतेत्यर्थः».

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this text is in the edition’s sources. The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa read the passage as a prayer to the supreme self with knowledge; Bhāskara speaks of becoming one with brahman («ब्रह्मीभूतस्तिष्ठामीति»). None of them argues it against another school, and Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not among the sources.

contemporary.text: The prayer gives the breaths back to the one they came from. Treating what one has — time, attention, the ability to act — as received rather than owned changes how it is used. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: What would it mean to offer back something you were given?
reflect.deeper: The text says this teaching should be given even to one who has not asked. When is it right to teach what was not requested?
reflect.practice: For one minute, notice your breath without changing it, as something received.

references.text: Sāyaṇa comments on this anuvāka as his 48, Bhāskara as his 48; the edition’s concordance maps both correctly.

The claims about the effects of teaching and reciting the trisuparṇa (destroying the sin of killing a brāhmaṇa, attaining soma, purifying a row of diners) are the text’s own and are reported as such. The commentators’ restriction of the teaching to brāhmaṇas is reported as theirs.

flags.note: At दुष्ष्वप्नहन्, the Ānandāśrama pariśiṣṭa text reads र for न (दुष्ष्वप्रह-); the third witness does not settle it (corrections.json, review). The base reading is kept; Sāyaṇa’s and Bhāskara’s glosses (‘slayer of evil dreams’) support it.
The word division brahmam etu (Sāyaṇa) against brahma metu (Bhāskara), and the reading of duruṣṣaha (imperative or adjective), are open.
